The shelving scheme the Library of Congress built around 1900 for its own collection, now used by most large research libraries in the United States.

## Twenty-one letters

It uses 21 single-letter classes (Q is science, T is technology, Z is bibliography) followed by a second letter and a number: QA76 is computer science. Because letters give up to 26 options per position, the top levels are wider and shallower than a ten-way split.

## Built from the books on hand

The classes were drafted from the books the library actually held, discipline by discipline, by different specialists. So the scheme is uneven by design: some areas are finely divided and others are coarse, matching where the collection was large.

## What I said reading it

Same bet as [[dewey-decimal-classification]]: a book lives in one place. The difference is only in how wide each level is.
